front: How does a retained log differ from a competing work queue?
back: A retained log supports independent progress and replay of ordered history; a work queue distributes tasks under acknowledgment or lease semantics. Inspect actual product behavior.

front: Which asynchronous boundaries should be distinguished?
back: Acceptance, durable append, delivery, processing, effect completion, and recorded progress.

front: Why is broker acceptance not proof that a document is searchable?
back: Chunking, embedding, indexing, version publication, and authorization may still be incomplete.

front: Why keep business event identity separate from log position?
back: A position identifies an append occurrence; multiple occurrences can represent one retried business event.

front: How should a partition key be chosen?
back: From the smallest business scope requiring order, balancing independent parallelism against cross-key invariants.

front: A hot key emits 7k/s to a 5k/s partition while fleet capacity is spare. What happens?
back: That partition backlog grows 2k/s; aggregate spare capacity cannot automatically process the same ordered key.

front: Why can increasing partition count disrupt application ordering?
back: Routing may move a key while old records remain elsewhere; a migration/version boundary is needed under the actual product contract.

front: Does ordered fetch imply ordered business completion?
back: No. Parallel workers may finish later records first; preserve per-entity order or enforce version preconditions.

front: Why is replication factor alone not a durability guarantee?
back: Acknowledgment thresholds, eligible replicas, placement, persistence assumptions, and recovery policy determine survival.

front: What does a lost append acknowledgment mean?
back: The append may already be durable. Retry under the supported transport identity and retain stable business identity.

front: What does producer idempotence not automatically cover?
back: Duplicate upstream business generation, a different producer incarnation outside its scope, or arbitrary external effects.

front: What are the two basic consumer progress crash windows?
back: Progress first can skip an unapplied effect; effect first can repeat after redelivery unless atomic or repeat-safe.

front: How can a database projection handle redelivery safely?
back: Commit the event marker and business update in the same transaction, scoped to the projection/effect namespace.

front: Why is a marker committed before the effect in another transaction unsafe?
back: A crash can leave a marker that makes replay skip an effect that never occurred.

front: Do broker transactions make a remote payment exactly once?
back: Not automatically. The external effect must cooperate through a supported atomic, idempotent, or reconcilable contract.

front: What does a safe scalar restart frontier represent?
back: A prefix whose work may safely be skipped under the declared processing and replay contract.

front: If 102 finishes before 100 and 101, can restart move to 103?
back: No. Under the contiguous-position model, advance only after the unfinished prefix is safely complete.

front: What can survive a consumer rebalance outside transport ownership?
back: Already-dispatched GPU work or external effects; group reassignment does not necessarily stop them.

front: Why separate long-running execution from broker discovery?
back: A durable task system can own leases, retries, and outputs independently of short consumer sessions.

front: What must replay define?
back: Purpose, effect/projection namespace, schema compatibility, authorization, retention/payload availability, and resource budgets.

front: What is end-to-end backpressure?
back: Downstream resource constraints change upstream production or admission across every buffering layer.

front: Why is a count-only queue bound insufficient for AI payloads?
back: Prompt and payload sizes vary; bytes, tokens, concurrency, and deadlines can dominate resources.

front: With 60k free queue slots and net growth 400 tasks/s, what is fill time?
back: 150 seconds under fixed-rate assumptions.

front: After a 90-second burst, why is the example backlog 56k?
back: It starts at 20k and grows by (1000−600)×90 = 36k.

front: How long to drain 56k when service is 600/s and new arrivals 400/s?
back: 280 seconds at net 200/s, assuming fixed rates and no other bottleneck.

front: Why can immediate retries defeat pressure controls?
back: They amplify offered load and can keep the system overloaded after original demand falls.

front: When should a credit be returned?
back: When the corresponding bounded resource is actually released, not merely when the client times out.

front: What does 50k records/s × 800 bytes imply?
back: 40 MB/s decimal logical stored-record data before replication and other overhead.

front: What is the example three-copy 24-hour record-data estimate?
back: 50,000×800×86,400×3 = 10.368 TB decimal, excluding overhead, reserve, and compression changes.

front: Why can a slow consumer lose replayability despite a time-retention setting?
back: Byte limits or expiry can remove needed records before repair and net catch-up finish.

front: Why is compaction not always a full event-history replacement?
back: Latest-per-key behavior can remove transitions a rebuild requires; actual tombstone and deletion semantics matter.

front: Should every poison event simply be skipped?
back: No. Skipping may violate entity order or security invariants; quarantine, pause, repair, and replay need explicit policy.

front: Why separate retrieval freshness from authorization revocation?
back: Delayed indexing may be acceptable while stale permission enforcement can expose data.

front: What can dynamic batching improve and worsen?
back: It can amortize execution cost but adds queue delay, memory pressure, and correlated batch failure/cancellation complexity.

front: What should pipeline observability measure beyond broker lag?
back: Accepted-to-usable freshness, bytes/time lag, hot keys, completion gaps, retries, uncertainty, retention headroom, and governed failures.
